title: Error handling: which net catches what

screens.prompt: In B9, price the code in A8 and say no match when any part of the lookup fails.

hints.syntax: =IFERROR(value, value_if_error) — two arguments, the second is the net.
hints.func-iferror: Any failure at all has to become the word no match, which is the wider net.
hints.func-vlookup: The price is in the second column of the table.
hints.require-ref: Read the code from the grid instead of typing it.
hints.value: Q-9 is not on the list, so the lookup fails with #N/A and the net catches it.
hints.error: IFERROR catches #DIV/0! as well, so a guarded division reports the net's word.

screens.prompt: In D8, divide the price on row 4 by its units and say no units when the division fails.

hints.syntax: =IFERROR(B3/C3,"no units") — the division sits inside the net.
hints.func-iferror: A blank divisor raises #DIV/0!, and the net is what turns it into a word.
hints.require-ref: Divide the price in the grid by the units in the same row.
hints.value: The units cell on row 4 is empty, so the division fails and the answer is no units.
hints.error: IFNA would not help here: #DIV/0! is not #N/A, so the error escapes it.

reject.why: IFNA catches #N/A only, so the division error escapes
the divisor comes from another row, so the answer is a number
row 3 is divided instead of the row the question names
the net catches the failure but prints the wrong word
the net's word is then divided by zero
the division sits outside the parentheses the function needs

docs.syntax: =IFERROR(value, fallback) catches everything; =IFNA(value, fallback) catches only #N/A
docs.explain: Two nets, two jobs. IFERROR evaluates its first argument and returns the second if any error at all comes back, which makes it the right choice when the question is whether a calculation worked at all — a division by an empty cell, a lookup into a range that is not there, text handed to arithmetic. IFNA is the narrower net: it returns the second argument only for #N/A, the error raised when a lookup or a match finds nothing, and lets every other error through. Choosing between them is a decision about what the sheet is going to say. A wide net makes the output tidy, and it also hides the bugs: a #REF! that should have been fixed at the source becomes a friendly word that looks like ordinary missing data. A narrow net keeps that distinction, at the cost of showing the rarer errors while the sheet is being built. In this drill the first screen prices Q-9, which is not on the list, so the wide net answers no match; the second divides a price by an empty units cell, where #DIV/0! is the error and IFNA would not have helped. Both screens put the net around the whole calculation rather than around one lookup, which is the shape that keeps working when the formula grows.

errors.text: What IFNA is for: the lookup found nothing.
A blank or zero divisor; IFERROR catches it, IFNA does not.
A reference outside the range; only the wide net catches it.

docs.atWork: Keeping a report tidy without hiding the broken references that need a real fix.
docs.outcome: Pick the wide or the narrow net deliberately, and put it around the whole calculation.
docs.teaches: IFERROR versus IFNA on a missing lookup and on a division by a blank cell
docs.dataset: Code, price and units table with one blank units cell
